Harris quotes the incorporation clause common to the Trent and Mersey and Staffordshire and Worcestershire acts of 1766 verbatim: 'one body politic and corporate . . . shall have perpetual succession, and shall have a common seal, and by the name shall and may sue and be sued, and also shall and may have power and authority to purchase lands' (98, quoting the preambles to 6 Geo. III c.96 and c.97). 'Body politic and corporate' is the tradition's own term for juridical personhood and it is the phrase the drafters used. General law to the same effect at 18: 'Incorporation involved the creation of a new personality, distinct from that of individual human beings', the dominant common-law conception being 'that of the State- or law-fabricated artificial person'. Measured negatively at 141: the unincorporated company 'was not a body politick and corporate' and 'could not be a corporate entity', because 'only the State, via the Crown or Parliament, could grant corporate status'; and at 146, where the separate entity defeated the Statute of Artificers apprenticeship objection and the five-assignee proviso on patents. SCOPE JUDGEMENT REQUIRED BY THE joint_stock ROW HEADER AND MADE HERE: every passage relied on bears on a CHARTERED entity. 98 is the text of two acts of incorporation; 18-19 is the law of corporations; 141 and 146 state what the unincorporated company lacked BY CONTRAST with the corporation. No cell of this row takes a value from a passage in which 'joint stock company' could mean the unincorporated form.

ARTICULATED. The same quoted 1766 clause confers 'power and authority to purchase lands . . . without incurring any of the penalties or forfeitures of the Statute of Mortmain' (98). General law at 19: 'A corporation could own (in the feudal sense) and convey land, at times with restrictions', the restriction being that only a mortmain licence in the charter or statute let it 'enjoy the privilege of perpetual ownership and exemption from dues'. THE MORTMAIN QUALIFICATION WAS CONSIDERED AND DOES NOT REDUCE THIS TO P: mortmain conditioned the perpetual holding of LAND against feudal dues, not the capacity to hold property in the entity's name, and the 1766 acts grant the licence in the same breath as the power. Corroborated at 145-146, where excise status and patent assignment turn on corporations being 'seen as legal entities separated from their members'. SCOPE: a quoted act of incorporation and the general law of corporations, both chartered.

ARTICULATED. 'by the name shall and may sue and be sued' - the quoted 1766 incorporation clause (98), and the same privilege expressly listed in the River Dun act of 1733 (94). General law at 19: 'The corporation did not have to litigate under its members' names, but could sue and be sued, for better or for worse, in its separate personality, in the same manner as individuals.' THE CONTRAST CASE MEASURES THE VALUE: at 144-145 all partners of an unincorporated company had to be joined, one debtor requiring twenty-five separate actions and 300 shareholders able to file 300 defences; at 165 unincorporated companies had to buy a private act to sue in an officer's name, thirty such acts by 1815. SCOPE: the quoted clauses are chartered or statutory instruments; 144-145 and 165 are cited for the contrast they draw, not for a value.

Harris denies in terms that the object had that shape in this period: 'it should not be assumed that the seventeenth or eighteenth centuries functioned under the modern perception of limitation of liability as a binary legal feature that a corporation or an era has or lacks. Limited liability in this period should not even be viewed as a continuum, but rather as a matrix with several dimensions' (129), those dimensions being which of three classes of debt, by what enforcement procedure, at what time, up to what portion, and jointly or severally (128-129). THREE FURTHER FACTS EACH INDEPENDENTLY BLOCK A VALUE. (i) The attribute is instrument-dependent, not formal: a corporation could make further calls on members to pay creditors only where 'call-making powers were explicitly given to that corporation in its act or charter of incorporation', and incorporation by Act carried limited liability only 'provided that an explicit clause to that affect was included in the incorporating statute' (129-130). (ii) IT IS EXPRESSLY OPTIONAL AFTER 1825, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE TEXTBOOK STORY: section 2 of the repeal act let the Crown 'declare and provide, that the members of such corporation shall be individually liable, in their persons and property, for the debts, contracts and engagements of such corporation' (6 Geo. IV c.92, quoted at 270-271), and its promoters 'envisioned an increase in chartered incorporation, yet in most cases without the privilege of limited liability' (271). (iii) The value would in any case change inside any period this row can claim - absent or incoherent to the 1780s, then 'relatively clear by 1825 that incorporation by charter carried with it limitation on the liability of the shareholders' (130) - and heterogeneity across time is the condition for splitting a row, never for P. SPLITTING DOES NOT RESCUE THE CELL, AND THAT IS THE POINT: on Harris's account owner shielding was at no date in scope an attribute of the FORM, only of the individual charter or act. ARTICULATED. 'shall have perpetual succession' - the quoted 1766 incorporation clause (98); the same three privileges are expressly listed in the River Dun act of 1733, 'perpetual succession, common seal, and the right to sue and be sued using the corporate name' (94). General law at 19: the corporation's 'legal personality did not terminate with the death of any human individual; it was potentially immortal and subject to dissolution only in a strictly defined manner'. Measured negatively at 78: undertakings not incorporated by charter or act 'could not enjoy the capacities and privileges of corporations as legal entities, including perpetual succession'. Contrast the partnership at 21 and 29, where the death, retirement or bankruptcy of one member ended the arrangement.

OPEN. TS1=1 constrains TS2 toward open and the evidence is direct: perpetual succession in the constitutive instruments (94, 98), potential immortality at 19, and the East India Company's movement 'from ad hoc per voyage capital (1-3 years, invested in specific ships), to capital for limited duration (8-15 years), and finally to permanent and continuous capital' (25), which is the endpoint the form carries into this row's period. AGAINST IT, AND CARRIED RATHER THAN CODED: the incorporation FRANCHISE was often term-limited - 'The State could, at will, withhold an incorporation franchise which, in many cases, was of limited duration' (113) - and the moneyed companies bought charter extensions (55 n 36). That is a term on the grant, not on the arrangement; the renewals were sought precisely to continue an undertaking with no internal end date. Confidence medium because Harris nowhere states the horizon as such and the value is assembled.

NOT REVOCABLE AT WILL. The corporation was 'subject to dissolution only in a strictly defined manner' (19). No member could unwind it: the contrast Harris draws with the partnership is that there the death, retirement or change of status 'of even one of its members signaled the end of the partnership' (21), and in the corporation it did not. THE SOVEREIGN'S POWER IS REAL AND IS NOT AT WILL: 'Unauthorized corporations could be dissolved and abused charters could be forfeited by the court' through quo warranto and scire facias (18) - forfeiture for cause, on judicial process. Eldon in 1825 held 'that if a company acted improperly a charter could be withdrawn immediately, whereas a company formed by an act could be deprived of its incorporation only by a repealing act' (260 n 29, and see 271); again for cause. Non-renewal of a term-limited franchise (113) is a refusal to continue, not a power to dissolve. ADJUDICATION FOR THE MAINTAINER: on a charter-only reading of the row Eldon's asymmetry would push toward P; the row as scoped includes companies incorporated by Act, the asymmetry is then heterogeneity across instruments rather than half-presence, and 0 holds.

STRUCTURAL HALF, AND THE HALVES ARE RULES AGAINST PURPOSE. Rules: a corporation 'could make bylaws to govern its internal affairs' (19), and the 1766 acts 'specify the capital to be raised by each company, its structure, future calls, voting rights, assemblies and committees, bylaws, officers, and more' (98) - internal rule-making is an incident of incorporation. Purpose: fixed by the charter or act and alterable only by a further grant - the Grand Junction's larger and more complex managerial and financial structure came from its own act of 1793 (99), and alterations to the East India Company's affairs came by statute (Dividend Act 1767, Regulation Act 1772, India Act 1784, at 206). One limb present, one absent, within one arrangement: P, not heterogeneity. The bylaw power was bounded in a way that matters to AP3: calls could not be imposed on members 'based on bylaws or directors' decisions' unless the charter or act gave the power (129).

COMMON. 'Unlike the regulated corporation, the joint-stock corporation traded in only one account. That meant that members shared not only overhead but all business activities of the corporation, that is, all profits and losses' (33). This is what distinguishes the joint-stock from the regulated corporation in Harris's own taxonomy, whose members 'traded in their own stock, taking risks and liabilities individually' (32) - a several-accounts arrangement in this vocabulary's terms. THE VALUE IS PERIOD-DEPENDENT AND IT IS RECORDED HERE BECAUSE IT BEARS ON THE ROW'S START DATE: before the 1620s the same corporations ran several-accounts capital - the Russia Company was reorganised in 1586 on 'short-term rather than perpetual capital organized in several separate accounts, each for a period of one to three years', and by 1622-1623 'the separate accounts were replaced by individual accounts' (45). A row starting at 1553 or 1600 would span two values of CI1. See the type row on period.

LOCKED IN, ON AN EXPRESS NEGATIVE COMPARISON. Of the cost book adventurer's exit right - 'to relinquish their interest upon written notice and withdraw their share in cash, whose value was usually left to arbitration' - Harris writes: 'This alternative was not available even in the joint-stock company' (191). SCOPE JUDGEMENT, REQUIRED BECAUSE 'joint-stock company' IS AMBIGUOUS IN THIS LITERATURE: the comparison set is fixed on the following page, where the cost book system is 'fundamentally different from the joint-stock corporation, from the common-law partnership, and from the unincorporated company' (192). The corporation is the intended term. Corroborated from the form's own history: the EIC's arrival at 'permanent and continuous capital', where 'only the profits were divided while the initial investment was retained by the company' (25), and the observation that the few joint-stock corporations formed after the Restoration 'were organized with permanent rather than ad hoc and dividable capital' (52). Exit is by SALE of the share, not by withdrawal of capital, which is why CI2 and CI3 are both 1. PERIOD-DEPENDENT: permanent stock 'turned out to be a problematic and undesirable feature for the early business corporations' and survived only in the EIC (45); a row starting before the 1680s would span. Confidence medium: one express sentence plus the capital history, with no clause quoted.

TRANSFERABLE. 'while interests in the joint-stock corporation were relatively freely transferable, in the partnership they were not' (33); 'every joint-stock corporation was inherently allowed to open public subscriptions, within or outside of the Stock Exchange' (114); and in practice 'transfer of shares was a simple selling transaction, normally completed smoothly, between two interested parties, under the auspices of the corporation' (118). Harris's own hedge is carried and not exceeded - 'relatively freely' - but he holds the legal doubts about the nature of the share not to have posed 'a major threat to actual transferability', for three stated reasons (118). Transferable joint stock is one of the four features by which he defines the form (22, 110).

STRUCTURAL HALF, AND THE HALF IS A DEFECT IN THE LAW OF THE SHARE RATHER THAN IN PRACTICE. For: the share circulated on a public market, quoted in the Course of the Exchange, sold between strangers under the corporation's auspices (114, 118). Against: 'corporate shares, which began circulating during that century, were a phenomenon novel and strange to the law', and the questions of what kind of property they were 'were not considered directly, and certainly not in an abstract manner, by the courts until the 1820s' (117-118); on three occasions shares in land-dominated corporations 'were viewed as real estate', which 'could lead to low transferability'; and what preserved negotiability was not the general law but 'a standard clause in most incorporation acts declar[ing] shares to be personal property' (118). An interest whose depersonalisation rests on a drafting clause and an unlitigated silence, rather than on a settled legal character, is half-depersonalised. CI4 entails CI3, and P beside CI3=1 is consistent with that direction of entailment.

Harris lists among the questions whose unsettledness makes the period's 'limited liability' incoherent exactly the one this column asks: 'what was the relationship between shareholders as far as debts were concerned? Were shareholders held in debt together or separately; that is to say, could the entire debt of a corporation be collected from one shareholder, or was each shareholder responsible only for his or her proportional share in the total debt?' (129). He does not answer it, and concludes that 'All these questions indicate that there was no coherent, well-defined conception of limited liability in late seventeenth-century England'. NOT RECORDED. LR2's locator is the decision-maker. Harris establishes that the corporation had 'concentration of management' and a 'hierarchical managerial structure' distinguishing it from the partnership (33, 22), and that directors' decisions could not by themselves impose calls on members (129); he nowhere asks whether directors or managers were exposed to the venture's gains and losses. He rules the question out of scope himself: this book 'deals with the formal institutional structure of managerial structure. It deals only briefly with the structure of share holding: the nominal price of individual shares, minimum and maximum limitations on holding of shares by individuals, voting rights attached to shares, and the actual spreading of shareholding in various types of associations' (23 n 20), and he sets the separation-of-ownership-and-control literature aside as 'less relevant to the earlier setting and the more basic questions in which I am interested' (22 n 19). Inferring coupling from the shareholders' residual claim at LR3 would be filling this column from the column next door.

SHARED PROPORTIONALLY. 'members shared not only overhead but all business activities of the corporation, that is, all profits and losses' (33). The claim is residual, not fixed, and it is what separates the joint-stock from the regulated corporation, whose members bore their own trading results individually (32). QUALIFICATIONS CARRIED RATHER THAN CODED: 'Even within the realm of corporate finance, corporate loans and preference shares played a role alongside ordinary shares' (127) - fixed claims existed beside the residual one, but as separate instruments held by separate claimants, not as the members' own entitlement; and statutory ceilings on the East India Company's dividends from 1767 (206) are a public-law constraint on distribution, not a change in the basis of the claim.

NOT POOLED, AND THE CONTRAST IS THE SOURCE'S OWN. Harris treats the mutual association as a distinct form and defines the difference on precisely this question: 'The major difference between mutuals and joint-stock companies was that the owners of mutuals (as their name suggests) were also the consumers or clients' - insurance offices 'in which the owners-insurers were also the insured', building societies 'in which the constructors would also be the residents of the dwellings they built', and loan banking 'in which the owners were to deposit and borrow' (36). In the proprietary joint-stock corporation the members are proprietors, and the risks the entity carries are the venture's, not the members' own separate risks: the Sun 'was based on proprietorship and joint stock, not on mutual principles. The insured persons were not necessarily members' (101). CONFIDENCE LOW AND THE ALTERNATIVE IS STATED FAIRLY: Harris also holds that mutuals 'could be organized under various schemes: as corporations or as unincorporated firms, with or without permanent joint stock' (33-36), so a chartered body could itself be a mutual. The value holds for the PROPRIETARY joint-stock corporation this row scopes, not for every chartered corporation. A maintainer who reads 33-36 as a taxonomy of forms rather than as evidence about this form should recode to .NR, which would carry LR5 with it. Flagged in the notes file.

MEMBERSHIP. The claim runs from being a member of a body corporate, not from a contract with it and not from a beneficial interest. The 1733 River Dun act 'united the undertakers into one Company and Copartnership as a Body Politick and Corporate' (94); Harris's contrast between regulated and joint-stock corporations is put throughout in terms of what 'members' of each shared (32-33); and his liability questions are questions about 'shareholders' as members of the corporation (128-129). Contrast the trust-based forms, where entitlement runs through trustees to beneficiaries and 'The property of the company was vested in trustees' (147) - a route this form does not use, which is also the boundary against deed_of_settlement_company.

COLLECTIVE, AND THE VALUE SET CANNOT RECORD WHAT HARRIS THINKS IMPORTANT ABOUT IT - FLAGGED, NOT REPAIRED. Decision-making sits with the members and the organs they constitute: corporations 'had a hierarchical structure, which included heads, officials, members, and assemblies (or at least some of these organs), and a formal decision-making process including the power to make bylaws, to hold internal tribunals, and the like' (23); the 1766 acts specify 'voting rights, assemblies and committees, bylaws, officers' (98); a corporation 'could make bylaws to govern its internal affairs' (19). It is neither founder-fixed nor single-principal, so collective is the only value that fits. THE GAP: managerial hierarchy is ONE OF HARRIS'S FOUR DEFINING FEATURES of the form (22, 110), and what he says distinguishes the corporation is that it had a 'legally enforced arrangement for appointment and delineation of responsibilities of officeholders, and for assemblies, reports, votes, and the like' where the partnership had none (144). MG2's three values record the LOCUS of decision and cannot record a delegated hierarchy under collective ultimate control, so 'collective' loses the feature the source insists on. Recorded here and argued in the notes file; NO characteristic is proposed, per the rule against proposing a repair in the batch that motivates it.

NOT RESTRICTED, FOR THE PERIOD THIS ROW CLAIMS. 'every joint-stock corporation was inherently allowed to open public subscriptions, within or outside of the Stock Exchange' (114), and shares moved by simple sale between strangers (118). MG1 is 'membership', so the cell is applicable. TWO COUNTER-INSTANCES ARE RECORDED RATHER THAN AVERAGED AWAY, AND BOTH LIE OUTSIDE OR AT THE EDGE OF THE PERIOD. (i) In the first age of the form, 'The typical charter of a business corporation limited its membership by demanding relatively high membership fees or a significant contribution to the joint stock of the corporation' (41) - a further characteristic that would span if this row began in the sixteenth or seventeenth century. (ii) The Amicable, incorporated by letters patent in 1706, had its letters patent 'limit the number of members to 2,000, and the number of shares per person to three' (101) - a chartered entity with numerically restricted membership, and a mutual. Membership size was fixed by the individual instrument where it was fixed at all; the general position after 1720 is open subscription. Confidence medium for that reason.

STATE-CHARTER, AND IT IS THE DEFINING RESTRICTION IN HARRIS'S OWN SUMMARY TABLE, which enters 'Can be formed only by state sanction' against the joint-stock business corporation (Table 1.1, 35). 'by the sixteenth century, an explicit, ex ante and direct authorization by the King became the only mode of incorporation. This authorization was normally given in the form of charter (or letters patent), and, occasionally, by way of Act of Parliament bearing the King's explicit consent, or a combination of an act and a charter' (17). Incorporation was 'an essential component of the King's exclusive and voluntary prerogative to create and grant dignities, jurisdictions, liberties, exemptions, and, in our case, franchises' (18). After the Glorious Revolution 'An act of Parliament, or a charter coupled with an act, became the more common method of forming a company, while incorporation only by charter became rare' (53) - a shift of instrument within one value. Coded analyst-imposed rather than articulated: the instruments name themselves charter, letters patent and act, but 'state-charter' is the census's category, not the tradition's word.

COMMERCIAL-PROFIT. 'The regulated corporation, like the joint-stock corporation, and unlike earlier corporations, was formed purely for business purposes and aimed at profit maximization' (32); 'The joint-stock corporation, like the regulated corporation and unlike other corporations, aimed at profit maximization' (33). Table 1.1 enters 'Profit' under Aim for the joint-stock business corporation without the partial-conformity marker Harris attaches to its Limited liability entry (34-35). The nonbusiness and nonprofit corporations and the charitable trusts are a separate category and are excluded (36).

STRUCTURAL HALF, AND THE HALVES ARE THE TWO LIMBS OF THE CHARACTERISTIC'S OWN WORDING: an exclusive right or franchise, held AS PROPERTY. Franchise: incorporation itself is a franchise in the King's gift (18), and chartered corporations held exclusive rights of several kinds - 'on overseas territories, over specified business activity (such as note issuing), and on the corporate form in a given sector (marine insurance), as well as natural monopolies (infrastructure and utilities)' (113). As property: denied in terms. 'Incorporation itself was not considered a protectable property right. The State could, at will, withhold an incorporation franchise which, in many cases, was of limited duration'; and 'Like incorporation, monopoly was not considered protected private property. . . . Throughout our period, monopolies were granted and abolished, either directly or by inference' (113). THE ALTERNATIVE READING, STATED FAIRLY: read as 'holds a trade monopoly', the value would be heterogeneous across instances rather than half-present - 'monopoly became an almost inherent characteristic of the early business corporations' (41), but 'monopoly privileges were no longer an essential part of every incorporation' after the 1680s (52), 'By 1800, most of the monopolies held by corporations were a thing of the past' (203), and the East India, Bank of England and marine insurance monopolies were abolished between 1813 and 1833 (287). Heterogeneity across instances is not P, which is why the value is taken on the property limb and not on that one.

STATUS ARBITRAGE, AND THE LEAD EVIDENCE IS NOT THE LIABILITY MATERIAL. At 146 the corporate form defeated two status-based disabilities outright: the Elizabethan Statute of Artificers apprenticeship requirement, where it was argued that all members of an association including passive investors had to have served apprenticeships - 'Such an argument could not have been raised against a business corporation, where the qualifications of the shareholders were not relevant to the status of the corporation vis-a-vis the Statute of Artificers'; and the proviso voiding patents assigned to more than five persons, from which 'Corporations, on the other hand, were not subject to such limitations because they were seen as legal entities separated from their members'. Excise rate turned on the same point at 145. CORROBORATION FROM THE STATUS OF THE MEMBER: an act of 1662 exempted shareholders of the East India, Guiney and Royal Fishing companies from bankruptcy procedures and was 'intended to protect noblemen, gentlemen and persons of quality' (128 n 38); by the end of the eighteenth century 'holding shares in a business corporation did not, in itself, turn a nontrader into a trader, subjecting him or her to bankruptcy law' (129), the trader line being the one that decided whether landed property was reachable and whether a man faced public examination and criminal prosecution (131). Contrast the sleeping partner, whose motive included avoiding 'the social stigma of the business' (30). Confidence medium: the value is assembled from four passages, none of which Harris frames as a single feature.

STRUCTURAL HALF, AND THE HALF IS CONSTITUTION WITHOUT RETURNS. Legible: the entity exists only by a public instrument of the State - charter, letters patent or act (17) - and that instrument specifies its capital, structure, calls, voting rights, assemblies, committees, bylaws and officers (98); Parliament legislated on named companies' internal affairs at will (206). Not registered: there was no register and no periodical return for chartered corporations before 1844. Harris's own account of 'The Rise of the Concept of Registration' shows the machinery being built everywhere ELSE first - ships (1786, 1825), savings banks (1817), joint-stock banks (1826), friendly societies (1829, 1834), building societies (1836), and companies formed by LETTERS PATENT SHORT OF INCORPORATION (1834, 1837, which did require six-monthly member lists open to inspection) - 'first employed in the context of ships, then friendly societies, savings and joint-stock banks, building societies, companies formed by letters patent, and only later on joint-stock companies of all sorts' (274-277). Registration for companies generally arrives with the act of 1844 (288), at this row's terminal date. THE CELL WOULD FLIP TO 1 AT 1844 BY DEFINITION - the same weakness the deed_of_settlement_company row records for its own FP4. Noted, not repaired.

NO CAPITAL-LABOUR ASYMMETRY. The joint-stock corporation's members are alike: all subscribe to one joint stock and 'members shared not only overhead but all business activities of the corporation, that is, all profits and losses' (33).
